title: Ruptured Ovarian Cyst and Acute Adnexal Pain: ED Assessment

evidenceAudit.scope: Premenopausal adult with acute adnexal pain in the emergency department (ED): pregnancy test first, ultrasound, ruptured or haemorrhagic cyst versus torsion, haemodynamic triage and surgical referral.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No national or specialty-society management guideline for ruptured ovarian cyst was opened; sources are a StatPearls review, an ACR imaging document, an ultrasound review and one single-centre retrospective study.
None of the sources gives analgesic doses or a transfusion threshold.
The conservative-versus-surgery criteria and risk factors come from one retrospective study (78 women) and need validation.
The ACR 2023 narrative sections were empty in the opened page; only variant ratings were read.
SFDA registration is not applicable because no medicine is prescribed here.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Functional follicular and corpus luteum cysts can bleed or rupture; corpus luteum cysts are more likely to haemorrhage. Rupture releases complex or echogenic free fluid; occasionally significant haemoperitoneum tracks into the upper abdomen. Significant blood loss can cause haemodynamic instability. Ovarian torsion is a separate gynaecological emergency and normal Doppler flow does not exclude it. A positive pregnancy test changes the pathway toward ectopic pregnancy.

symptoms: Unilateral lower abdominal pain, sudden and sharp.
Irregular menses or abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Pain after strenuous activity or intercourse.
physicalSigns: Tachycardia, hypotension or low diastolic pressure with significant bleeding.
redFlags: Severe or persistent pain despite analgesia, falling haemoglobin or increasing haemoperitoneum on repeat imaging.
Cyst over 10 cm, complex multilocular mass, solid components, thick septations, ascites or increased Doppler vascularity: suspect a neoplasm.
precipitants: Rapid growth or haemorrhage of a functional cyst.
Corpus luteum cysts (more likely to haemorrhage).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Positive β-human chorionic gonadotrophin (β-hCG); a ruptured haemorrhagic cyst was found at laparoscopy for suspected ectopic in one reported case.
Doppler flow can be normal (27% of left and 61% of right torsion cases); suspicion alone is a surgical indication.

differentials.condition: Pelvic inflammatory disease or urinary tract infection or stone

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: ACR variants 3–4 favour abdominal and pelvic ultrasound; computed tomography (CT) may be appropriate when β-hCG is negative.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Test first in every premenopausal patient; a positive result changes the imaging pathway.

clinicalManagement.title: Triage and stabilise
actions: Check vital signs; significant blood loss can cause haemodynamic instability.
If unstable, arrange urgent gynaecology or surgical review; laparotomy is usually preferred in unstable patients.

clinicalManagement.title: Pregnancy test first
actions: Do a urine or serum β-hCG in every premenopausal patient before imaging choices.
If positive, follow the ectopic pregnancy pathway; ultrasound (duplex Doppler adnexa, transabdominal, transvaginal) is usually appropriate and MRI and CT are usually not.

clinicalManagement.title: Image
actions: Transvaginal ultrasound first with Doppler; look for lace-like reticulation, retracting clot and echogenic free fluid.
Add haemoglobin; urinalysis and endocervical swabs for alternative causes.
Do not use normal Doppler flow to exclude torsion.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose conservative care or surgery
actions: Stable with mild-to-moderate symptoms: manage expectantly with observation of vital signs and haemoglobin, and repeat imaging if bleeding is suspected.

Surgery (all operations were laparoscopic in the cited study; laparotomy is usually preferred if the patient is unstable) for unstable vital signs, significant haemoglobin fall or increasing haemoperitoneum, severe or persistent pain despite analgesics, suspected torsion or suspected malignancy.
Significant blood loss may need admission, surgical evacuation and transfusion.

clinicalManagement.title: Follow-up
actions: Asymptomatic unilocular cyst under 10 cm: serial transvaginal ultrasound; persistence after several cycles needs further workup.
Endometrioma: ultrasound 6 to 12 weeks after the first scan; refer cysts with malignant features.

medicationPlan.note: None of the sources opened gives analgesic doses or a transfusion threshold. Follow the emergency department analgesia protocol and the hospital major-haemorrhage and blood transfusion policy.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Unstable vital signs, significant haemoglobin fall or increasing haemoperitoneum, or severe persistent pain despite analgesia.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Risk factors for surgery in one retrospective study
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Diastolic pressure 70 mmHg or lower and total pelvic fluid depth 5.6 cm or more; surgery rate 6.5% with neither, 15.8% with one, 77.8% with both.
Under 10 cm is usually benign; serial transvaginal ultrasound if asymptomatic.

guidelineComparison.title: Role of CT and MRI in acute adnexal pain

values: Transvaginal ultrasound first line; MRI or CT not recommended for initial evaluation.
Ultrasound usually appropriate in all variants.
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast may be appropriate (gynaecological) or usually appropriate (non-gynaecological suspicion).
Pelvic MRI may be appropriate when β-hCG is negative; usually not appropriate when positive.

guidelineComparison.note: Shown side by side and not merged; the pregnancy test decides which applies.

teaching.scope: Premenopausal adult with acute adnexal pain in the emergency department (ED): pregnancy test first, ultrasound, ruptured or haemorrhagic cyst versus torsion, haemodynamic triage and surgical referral.
learningObjectives: Triage between conservative care and surgery using haemodynamics, haemoglobin and imaging.
pitfalls: Discharging without a repeat haemoglobin after rupture with free fluid.
Over-relying on one retrospective study's thresholds.
keyPoints: Pregnancy test is the first test.
Normal Doppler does not exclude torsion.
Most stable ruptured cysts are managed expectantly.

patientEducation: Return for worsening pain, faintness, heavy bleeding or fever.
Explain that most functional cysts resolve on their own.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid strenuous activity and intercourse until pain settles, as advised by the treating team.
mdtReferrals: Gynaecology; general surgery if non-gynaecological cause; radiology; gynaecological oncology for cysts with malignant features.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamically stable with stable haemoglobin on repeat testing.
Safety-net advice and follow-up imaging booked where needed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Repeat ultrasound for persistent or complex cysts (endometrioma at 6 to 12 weeks, dermoid yearly); gynaecology review for any red-flag feature.
